seward.heading: Begin at the water. Follow the first mile.
seward.orientation: Southern gateway / Resurrection Bay / town-based heritage

experiences.title: Walk the first mile
experiences.copy: Start at the Trail Blazers statue outside the Alaska SeaLife Center and follow the waterfront path with the Seward Trailblazers' walking brochure.

experiences.title: See a port in the trail's story
experiences.copy: Seward became a winter port for the Iditarod gold fields. The town's waterfront provides a starting point for understanding the movement of mail, supplies and people inland.

experiences.title: Look from the present into the past
experiences.copy: Pair contemporary waterfront views with dated archival photographs, then follow the trail north through the map.

planning: Begin with a town-based outing. The waterfront walk is different from attempting remote sections of the historic trail.
Check local access and weather before a walk, especially when snow or ice changes the waterfront.
Check current visitor information before adding a museum visit or an onward trip to your day.
seward.history: Seward was founded in 1903 as the ocean terminus of the Alaska Central Railway. Gold discoveries in the Iditarod country made it a winter port for inland travel; its place in the national historic trail is commemorated at Mile Zero.

chugach.heading: Choose your way into Crow Pass country.
chugach.orientation: Southcentral Alaska / Girdwood and Eagle River / summer hiking

experiences.title: Start with a shorter outing
experiences.copy: The official trail guide allows for shorter day trips from either end. Choose a turnaround that suits your group and current conditions.

experiences.title: Read the landscape
experiences.copy: The historic supply route passes mining remains, alpine terrain and glacier views before descending toward the Eagle River valley.

experiences.title: Watch wildlife from a distance
experiences.copy: Carry binoculars and look for mountain wildlife without leaving designated trails or approaching animals.

planning: Summer focus: Alaska Fish & Game recommends June through September. Winter and spring bring high avalanche risk.
The full crossing generally takes two or more days. Access is from Crow Creek Trailhead near Girdwood or Eagle River Nature Center.
The through-route includes unbridged river fords. Consult the official guide and current land-manager information; cold water and mountain weather require serious preparation.

winter-trail.heading: A winter landscape. A journey to prepare for.
winter-trail.orientation: Across the historic trail / winter travel / remote routes

experiences.title: Understand the winter connection
experiences.copy: Frozen ground and waterways have long connected communities across this landscape. The historic trail remains a route for local travel as well as recreation.

experiences.title: Choose a route with local guidance
experiences.copy: Skiing, dog teams, snowmachines and fat-tire bicycles each require a plan suited to the particular route, land ownership and conditions.

experiences.title: Explore the history before the journey
experiences.copy: Read maps and firsthand accounts, then decide which part of the trail matches your experience and preparation.

planning: Remote sections demand a high level of self-reliance and proficiency in extreme winter travel and camping.
The historic trail crosses multiple landowners. A line on an orientation map is not a guarantee of access or current travel conditions.
Check current information with the relevant land manager and local community before setting out.

sections.title: Connections before the gold rush
sections.copy: Parts of the later Iditarod route followed travel networks used by Alaska Native communities long before the gold rush. The trail's history begins with those living connections.

sections.title: Mail, supplies and places to stop
sections.copy: Winter routes carried people, mail and supplies between coastal ports and Interior communities. Roadhouses became important stopping places along the route and its branches.

sections.title: Listen to the people who kept it
sections.copy: UAF's Iditarod National Historic Trail Project Jukebox preserves oral histories about designation, protection and cooperative management. The Alliance funded the project, completed in 2026.

a-living-connection.map_note: The main historic alignment connects a much wider network of communities and trails. This is an orientation map.

links.title: Listen to the trail’s oral histories

sections.title: When the landscape connects
sections.copy: The trail is primarily a winter route. Frozen ground changes the possibilities of travel across wetlands, rivers and mountain country.

sections.title: A continuing relationship
sections.copy: Local travel, dog teams and modern winter recreation are different parts of the trail's continuing life. Conditions and land ownership shape each journey.

sections.title: Read the trail before traveling it
sections.copy: Preparation begins with reliable maps, local knowledge and a realistic understanding of winter skills. Remote sections call for substantial self-reliance.

the-winter-way.map_note: The main historic alignment connects a much wider network of communities and trails. This is an orientation map.

links.title: Plan with the Bureau of Land Management

sections.title: A classroom rooted in place
sections.copy: Iditarod Trail to Every Classroom links educators, communities and the natural and cultural resources of the trail through place-based learning and stewardship.

sections.title: Learning becomes stewardship
sections.copy: Junior Trailblazer materials invite children and adults to explore historic and present-day uses of the trail. The booklet was developed with BLM Alaska and Chugach National Forest.

sections.title: Make a connection of your own
sections.copy: A place name, a local story or a trail visit can become a starting point for curiosity and care. Use the Alliance's learning resources to take the next step.

links.title: Explore Iditarod Trail to Every Classroom

alliance.intro: The work extends from recognizing historic places to supporting trail projects, education, and the preservation of first-person accounts.
alliance.timeline_heading: A long history. A shared responsibility.

timeline.title: A national historic trail
timeline.copy: Congress designates the Iditarod National Historic Trail. The designation recognizes a historic trail network; it is separate from the modern sled dog race.

timeline.title: The Alliance is founded
timeline.copy: A statewide nonprofit forms to advance knowledge, appreciation and enjoyment of the historic trail.

timeline.title: A centennial, shared
timeline.copy: The Alliance and its partners commemorate the trail's centennial and bring its history to wider audiences.

timeline.title: Marking the way
timeline.copy: Alliance funding helps community partners and BLM install a system of mileage, place-name and directional signs between the Alaska Range and Yukon River.

timeline.title: Voices preserved for the future
timeline.copy: UAF announces completion of the Alliance-funded Iditarod National Historic Trail Project Jukebox, preserving oral histories of trail protection and cooperative management.

work_themes.title: Care for the physical trail
work_themes.copy: The Alliance supports work with partners on the ground. Its documented projects include funding for 2013 waymarking and a 2014 repair effort near Farewell Lake after fire and erosion damaged the route.

work_themes.title: Keep the voices and records
work_themes.copy: Preservation includes the stories of people who protected, marked and managed the trail. The Alliance funded UAF's Iditarod National Historic Trail Project Jukebox, completed in 2026.

work_themes.title: Make learning a form of stewardship
work_themes.copy: Iditarod Trail to Every Classroom connects place-based learning, communities and public lands. Junior Trailblazer materials invite families to explore the trail's history and continuing use.
